extracted.intended_audience: writers, translators, students of literature, and learned readers
extracted.subtask_description: Practical principles and evaluative criteria for literary composition, diction, study habits, and translation (especially poetic translation), drawn from 18th‑century critical essays. Covers balancing fidelity and spirit in translation, matching diction to audience, and study methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value originals over imitations
rubrics_metrics.description: “Many of the works which time has left us, we know to have been these that were most esteemed, and which antiquity itself considered as models; so that, having the originals, we may without much regret lose the imitations.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer studying the original works that antiquity regarded as models rather than later imitations. Originals provide the authoritative forms and general tendencies of a piece; losing derivative or secondary versions is less harmful to literary understanding. Anti-pattern: treating slavish modern imitations as equivalent substitutes for primary models.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leave room for modern originality
rubrics_metrics.description: If all the writings of the ancients had remained, "almost every subject would have been pre-occupied, and every style would have been fixed by a precedent from which few would have ventured to depart."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that having too many authoritative precedents can stifle modern genius; originality and new industry require open subjects and flexible styles. As a creative principle, do not overvalue exhaustive antecedents to the point of discouraging innovation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance methodical study with serendipity
rubrics_metrics.description: “This opinion is, perhaps, generally true; yet ... it may be doubted whether the faculties may not be contracted by confining the attention ... Acquisitions of knowledge, like blazes of genius, are often fortuitous.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While a settled, methodical plan helps progress, allow space for unexpected discoveries and detours: accidental readings or chance encounters can open productive new directions. Practical application: keep a plan but follow promising attractions when they arise. Anti-pattern: rigidly adhering to a reading list that prevents following a genuinely stimulating detour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow productive inclination over rote plan
rubrics_metrics.description: “He who finds himself strongly attracted to any particular study, though it may happen to be out of his proposed scheme, if it is not trifling or vicious, had better continue his application to it, since it is likely that he will...attain that which a warm inclination stimulates him to pursue, than that at which a prescribed law compels him to toil.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When an interest strongly motivates you and leads to substantive progress, pursue it even if it diverges from your original plan—provided it is worthwhile. Example: abandoning a strict revision schedule to follow a burst of creative or scholarly insight. Scoring note: value demonstrated engagement and results over strict adherence to a plan.

rubrics_metrics.name: Translation: balance fidelity of sense with freedom of spirit (Dryden's principle)
rubrics_metrics.description: “Dryden saw very early that closeness best preserved an author's sense, and that freedom best exhibited his spirit; he, therefore, will deserve the highest praise, who can give a representation at once faithful and pleasing, who can convey the same thoughts with the same graces, and who, when he translates, changes nothing but the language.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim to preserve both meaning and the original's aesthetic or rhetorical spirit. Use closeness to safeguard precise sense and freedom to render tone, rhythm, and elegance. Anti-patterns: slavish literalism that loses poetic force (e.g., Chaucer degrading verse to prose) or reckless liberty that misstates sense. Practical test: does the translation read as the same work in the target language—same thoughts, same graces?

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetic translation should not be bound to original line counts
rubrics_metrics.description: Historical prejudice insisted that “the lines should be neither more nor fewer than those of the original”; critics later praised attempts to "break the boundaries of custom" and assert the "natural freedom of the Muse."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not insist on preserving the original poem's line count or line-for-line rhyme if doing so sacrifices natural English expression or the poem's spirit. Prioritize fluency, tone, and poetic effect in the target language. Anti-pattern: forcing line-for-line correspondence and thus producing awkward, cramped verse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observe a mean between literalness and paraphrase
rubrics_metrics.description: “There is undoubtedly a mean to be observed. Dryden...closeness best preserved an author's sense, and that freedom best exhibited his spirit...the paraphrastick liberties have been almost universally admitted.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seek a middle path: neither slavish literalness nor licentious re-writing. Gauge each passage—when precise diction is essential, be closer; when spirit, imagery, or meter must be conveyed, allow freedom. Scoring guidance: translations that both communicate accurate sense and read as artful compositions in the target language are highest rated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid voluntary obscurity and gratuitous hard words
rubrics_metrics.description: “If an author be supposed to involve his thoughts in voluntary obscurity, and to obstruct, by unnecessary difficulties, a mind eager in pursuit of truth...he counteracts the first end of writing, and justly suffers the utmost severity of censure.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not use obscure or grandiloquent words merely to impress; clarity is a primary aim of writing. Anti-pattern: writers who boast learning by making prose unintelligible. Exception: when addressing a specialist audience, technical terms may be appropriate (see next criterion).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use technical terms of art when necessary for precision
rubrics_metrics.description: “Every hour produces instances of the necessity of terms of art...Those, whose studies or employments force them upon closer inspection, must have names for particular parts, and words by which they may express various modes of combination...”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specialized vocabulary is justified where precision requires it (architecture, medicine, philosophy, etc.). But avoid needlessly obtruding jargon on general readers; adapt terminology to the audience. Anti-pattern: addressing incidental inquirers with the register reserved for fellow practitioners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match complexity and exposition to intended readership
rubrics_metrics.description: “Every author does not write for every reader...Diffusion and explication are necessary to the instruction of those...who can learn only what is expressly taught; but they who...are best pleased with involution of argument and compression of thought...”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide whether your audience is general or specialized and adjust exposition accordingly: more explanation and expanded argument for lay readers; compressed, nuanced expression for learned readers. Scoring note: appropriateness of register and depth to audience is a key evaluative criterion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Translate to widen access to knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: “Among the studies...none has been more diligently or more successfully cultivated than the art of translation; by which the impediments which bar the way to science are, in some measure, removed, and the multiplicity of languages become less incommodious.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One of translation's central aims is accessibility: render ideas so they can inform readers who lack the original language. Practical implication: prioritize communicative clarity and faithful transmission of knowledge in scholarly or scientific translation projects; in literary translation, balance accessibility with aesthetic fidelity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Renew impressions to retain ideas (memory and forgetfulness)
rubrics_metrics.description: “Forgetfulness is necessary to remembrance. Ideas are retained by renovation of that impression which time is always wearing away, and which new images are striving to obliterate.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For writers and students: to retain learnt material and creative ideas, periodically renew exposure and rehearsal. Practical techniques: revision, re-reading, notes, active use of ideas. Anti-pattern: one-off exposure expecting permanent retention without review.
